name: AP Statistics
overview: AP Statistics is a non-calculus introductory college statistics course built on four themes: exploring data, planning studies, using probability to model random behavior, and drawing statistical inferences. The exam rewards precise communication in context: describing distributions with shape, center, variability, and unusual features; naming the correct inference procedure and checking its conditions; interpreting intervals, P-values, and regression output; and explaining why conclusions follow (or don't) from how data were collected.
examMode: Hybrid digital: multiple-choice is taken in the Bluebook app; free-response questions are viewed in Bluebook and answers are handwritten in a paper booklet (confirm the current format on AP Central).

sections.name: Section I
sections.notes: Many questions are built on computer output, graphs, tables, or study descriptions. A formula sheet and tables (standard normal, t, chi-square) are provided.

sections.name: Section II
sections.questionType: Free response: 5 short questions + 1 investigative task
sections.notes: Q1–Q5 take about 13 minutes each; Q6, the investigative task, takes about 25 minutes and applies skills in a new way. Q1–Q5 count 75% of the section and Q6 counts 25%.

units.title: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions

skills.name: 1. Selecting Statistical Methods
skills.description: Choose appropriate methods for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data, including the correct inference procedure.

skills.name: 2. Data Analysis
skills.description: Describe patterns, trends, associations, and relationships in data, in context.

skills.name: 3. Using Probability and Simulation
skills.description: Explore random phenomena with probability models, simulation, and distributions.

skills.name: 4. Statistical Argumentation
skills.description: Develop explanations or justify conclusions using evidence from data, definitions, or inference.

scoring.summary: Section I (40 MCQ, no guessing penalty) and Section II are each 50% of the composite. Each FRQ is scored holistically 0–4 (E = essentially correct, P = partially correct, I = incorrect on each part, combined into a score). Context and communication count: a correct number with no context or a missing condition check usually drops a part from E to P.

frqTypes.name: Short FRQ (Q1–Q5)
frqTypes.howScored: Holistic 0–4 built from E/P/I on each part. Typical focuses: Q1 exploring data, Q2 collecting data (sampling or experimental design), Q3 probability and sampling distributions, Q4 inference, Q5 a combination of topics.

frqTypes.name: Investigative Task (Q6)
frqTypes.howScored: Holistic 0–4; extends familiar skills to an unfamiliar method or setting, often defining a new statistic or procedure in the question. Worth 25% of the free-response section.

strategy: Always answer in context: name the variable, the units, and the population.

For any inference question, use the four steps: State (parameter and hypotheses or confidence level), Plan (name the procedure and check Random, Independence/10%, and Normal/Large Counts), Do (test statistic, df, P-value or interval), Conclude (in context, linked to α or the interval).
Describe distributions with SOCS: Shape, Outliers/unusual features, Center, Spread, using numbers and comparative language when comparing groups.

Interpret a confidence interval: 'We are C% confident that the interval from __ to __ captures the true [parameter in context].' Interpret the level: in repeated samples, about C% of intervals capture the parameter.
Never 'accept' H₀. Say 'there is not convincing evidence that…'.
Identify random sampling (→ generalize to the population) separately from random assignment (→ cause-and-effect).
Show the formula with numbers substituted, or name the calculator function with all inputs labeled; bare calculator answers lose credit.
On Q6, read every part before starting; later parts often depend on a new statistic defined in early parts.
pitfalls: Interpreting a P-value as the probability that H₀ is true.
Writing hypotheses in terms of statistics (p̂, x̄) instead of parameters (p, μ).
Saying a large sample makes the population Normal; the CLT is about the sampling distribution.
Claiming causation from an observational study.
Using a two-sample procedure on paired data, or vice versa.
Interpreting r² or the slope without context, or the y-intercept when x = 0 is outside the data.
Treating 'not significant' as proof of no effect.
Confusing Type I (rejecting a true H₀) and Type II (failing to reject a false H₀) errors and their consequences.
referenceSheet: Provided in both sections: descriptive statistics (x̄, s, ŷ = a + bx, b = r·s_y/s_x, a = ȳ − b·x̄); probability (P(A ∪ B), P(A | B), mean and SD of discrete random variables, binomial P(X = x) = C(n,x)pˣ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ with μ = np and σ = √(np(1 − p)), geometric P(X = x) = (1 − p)ˣ⁻¹p with μ = 1/p and σ = √(1 − p)/p); sampling distributions and inference (statistic ± (critical value)(SE), standardized test statistic = (statistic − parameter)/SE, chi-square = Σ(observed − expected)²/expected, and the standard error for every procedure: one and two proportions, one and two means, slope); tables for standard normal probabilities, t critical values, and chi-square critical values.
